Rime (fog frozen onto trees and fences) and hoarfrost are both pruīna; Latin doesn’t distinguish them. Comenius: rōs congelātus pruīna dīcitur (Orbis pictus 7). aestuōsus, aestuōsa, aestuōsum — sultry, sweltering (Traupman 136): aestuōsa et pulverulenta via (Cic. Att. 5.14, cited by L&S). Morgan–Owens gives caelum crassum for humid air (M-O s.v. humidity, from Cic. Fat. 7); the Vatican lexicon gives āeris crassitūdō for muggy heat.
tepidus, tepida, tepidum — warm, mild; tepēscit — it is getting warm (Traupman 137).
frīgora, frīgorum n. pl. — cold spell (Traupman 135).

rōs, rōris m. — dew (Traupman 135).
gelārī; glaciārī — freeze, turn to ice (Traupman 135, 331); Morgan–Owens gives gelū concrēscere and conglaciāre (M-O s.v. freeze; Cic. N.D. 2.26). rigēns, rigentis — frozen stiff (Traupman 135).
Aquilō flat; pilleum indue. — The north wind is blowing; put your hat on.
Ecce, stīriae dē tēctō pendent! — Look, icicles hanging from the roof!
Herba rōre madet. — The grass is wet with dew.
Aestuō, tata! — I’m hot, Dad!

items.html: mūgiō, mūgīre, mūgīvī (mūgiī), mūgītum — moo, low (Traupman 142, 298): cum āctae bovēs mūgīssent (Liv. 1.7, as cited by L&S).
bālō, bālāre — bleat, of sheep, goats and lambs (Traupman 143–144; Plaut.; Ov.).
hinniō, hinnīre — neigh (Traupman 143; Quint. 7.3.3).
grunniō, grunnīre — grunt, oink (Traupman 143–144; Varr.).
glōciō, glōcīre — cluck (Traupman 141; Col. 8.5.4).

Quid dīcit vacca? — Mū! Vacca mūgit. — What does the cow say? — Moo! The cow is mooing.
Audīn' asinum rudentem? — Can you hear the donkey braying?
Rānae coaxant; fortasse pluet. — The frogs are croaking; maybe it’ll rain.

blocks.html: Not recommended: Traupman’s tetrinniō (quack), mintriō (squeak) and crocitāre are attested only in the late Carmen dē Philomēlā. His bombilāre (buzz), būbilāre (hoot) and gingrīre (cackle) are not Lewis & Short headwords (L&S has bombītāre, from the same late poem). For geese, owls and ducks, a plain verb such as clāmat or strīdet (Traupman 142) does the job.

keywords: zoo animals tiger panther leopard giraffe camel crocodile hippo hippopotamus rhino rhinoceros ostrich zebra dinosaur

items.html: tigris, tigris or tigridis m./f. — tiger (Traupman 145; Verg.; Plin.); panthēra, panthērae f. — panther, leopard (Traupman 138, 143); pardus, pardī m. — leopard (Traupman 143).
camēlopardalis, camēlopardalis f. — giraffe (Traupman 143, 321; Plin.: the “camel-leopard”); camēlus, camēlī m. — camel (Traupman 141).
crocodīlus, crocodīlī m. — crocodile (Traupman 142); hippopotamus, hippopotamī m. — hippopotamus (Traupman 143; Plin.); rhīnocerōs, rhīnocerōtis m. — rhinoceros (Traupman 144; Plin.; Mart.).
strūthiocamēlus, strūthiocamēlī m. — ostrich (Traupman 143; Plin.).
zebra, zebrae f. — zebra (Traupman 138, in the zoo dialogue: tigrēs et zebrās); not in Lewis & Short, a modern word. dinosaurus, dinosaurī m. — dinosaur (Traupman 304, modern).
Ecce camēlopardalis! Quam longō collō est! — Look, a giraffe! What a long neck it has!
Hippopotamus in aquā dormit. — The hippo is asleep in the water.

blocks.html: Lewis & Short marks the first vowel of tigris as doubtful; it is left unmarked. zebra and dinosaurus have no ancient quantity.

items.html: bellis, bellidis f. — daisy (Traupman 300; Plin. 26.26).
papāver, papāveris n. — poppy (Traupman 363; M-O s.v. poppy; Verg.; Plin.).
aphaca, aphacae f. — dandelion (M-O s.v. dandelion, citing Plin. 21.89 and André’s identification; L&S: “the common dandelion”).
hēlianthus, hēlianthī m. — sunflower (M-O s.v. sunflower; Linnaeus’s genus name, a modern coinage).

viola, violae f. — violet; līlium, līliī n. — lily; urtīca, urtīcae f. — nettle (Catull. 44.15); glāns, glandis f. — acorn. These are classical words from Lewis & Short; neither book has them in the sections swept.
Cavē urtīcās: urunt! — Mind the nettles: they sting!
Ecce, bellidēs in prātō! — Look, daisies in the meadow!
Glandēs sub quercū legāmus. — Let’s pick up acorns under the oak.
